hypothesis: If the permanent spiral forms of organisms (ruminant horns, molluscan and foraminiferal shells, sunflower capitula) are logarithmic spirals, then for any such structure the linear size of the growing edge (radius vector or whorl size) must increase exponentially with angle of rotation about the spiral's pole, r = a e^(b theta), and must do so better than the alternative simple spirals (Archimedean r = a + b theta, which grows linearly; Fermat / parabolic r = a sqrt(theta + theta0), which decelerates).
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. Only the molluscan-shell class can be tested with public data located (see interpretation). For every gastropod specimen in Collins et al. 2021 with >= 5 digitised successive half-whorl apertures, take the square root of aperture area as the linear whorl size at angles 0, pi, 2 pi, ...; for every ammonoid species in Korn & Walton 2018 with >= 5 half-whorl diameters, take conch diameter at each half whorl. Fit the three two-parameter models by least squares in the size domain and compare root-mean-square residuals. The claim (for molluscan shells) is supported if the logarithmic model has the lowest RMSE in >= 80% of gastropod specimens and in >= 80% of ammonoid species, and the median ratio RMSE(Archimedean) / RMSE(logarithmic) exceeds 1.5 in both groups. Because horns, foraminifera and sunflower capitula remain untested, the confidence attached to a supporting verdict is capped at 0.5.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted (for molluscan shells, and hence as a universal) if the logarithmic model is best in fewer than 50% of specimens in either group, or if the median RMSE ratio Archimedean / logarithmic is below 1.0 in either group. Intermediate results are 'mixed'.
interpretation: Thompson's statement is a universal over four classes of structure plus a stated exception (the cordate leaf). Public coordinate data were found only for molluscan shells: no digitised floret positions of sunflower capitula (the Swinton et al. 2016 citizen-science deposit gives parastichy counts and annotated photographs, not coordinates), no horn centre-line or outline data, and no foraminiferal chamber-position tables were located on Dryad, Zenodo or figshare; MorphoSource meshes require a login. The test therefore covers only the molluscan class, and its verdict is explicitly a test of that class with the caveat that a logarithmic fit for molluscs cannot establish the universal. 'Logarithmic spiral' is operationalized as exponential growth of linear whorl size with rotation angle: in a gastropod, the square root of aperture area at successive half whorls; in an ammonoid, conch diameter at successive half whorls (for a planispiral conch the diameter is the sum of two opposite radius vectors and grows exponentially if and only if the radius does). Both datasets were already downloaded for claim tests thompson1917-ch11-05 and thompson1917-ch11-15; those tests examined allometry of conch proportions and whorl-expansion and apical angles, not the comparison of spiral models made here.

datasets.name: Data associated with: Going round the twist - An empirical analysis of shell coiling in helicospiral gastropods (Collins, Klapaukh, Crampton, Gazley, Schipper, Maksimenko, Hines 2021, Paleobiology)
datasets.role: sectioned_shells.tps inside the archive: aperture outlines (50 semilandmarks) every 180 degrees for 184 gastropod specimens of 29 species; 145 specimens (21 species) have >= 5 apertures

datasets.name: Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn 2018, Palaeontology)
datasets.role: 'dm' sheet: conch diameter at every half whorl (median 16 stages, ~0.5 to ~30 mm) for 179 planispiral ammonoid species

method: For 145 gastropod specimens (>= 5 apertures) the series sqrt(aperture area in mm^2) versus angle (0, pi, 2pi, ...) and for 179 ammonoid species the series conch diameter versus whorl angle were each fitted by nonlinear least squares with a logarithmic spiral a e^(b theta), an Archimedean spiral a + b theta and a Fermat spiral a sqrt(theta + theta0); the model with the lowest RMSE was recorded per series and the median RMSE ratios Archimedean/logarithmic and Fermat/logarithmic computed per group. Pre-registered thresholds were then applied.

measured.unit: fraction of gastropod specimens for which the logarithmic spiral has the lowest RMSE (ammonoids: 1.000)
measured.uncertainty: gastropods n = 145 specimens / 21 species; ammonoids n = 179 species

gastropod_species_where_Archimedean_fits: Pelicaria vermis (36 specimens, log best in 14%)

caveats: Only the molluscan-shell class of Thompson's universal was tested; ruminant horns, foraminiferal shells and sunflower capitula (and the cordate-leaf exception) remain untested for lack of public coordinate data, so even a clean pass could not have established the universal claim.

Within molluscs the result is itself mixed: every one of 179 ammonoid species is fitted far better by the logarithmic spiral (median RMSE ratio 15 against Archimedean), but only 68% of gastropod specimens (14 of 21 species) are, and in the Struthiolariidae genus Pelicaria (36 specimens) and a handful of other species the whorl size grows closer to linearly than exponentially with angle over the digitised whorls. Collins et al. (2021) themselves report that struthiolariid coiling departs from constant-rate (logarithmic) growth.

Gastropod series are short (median 8 half-whorl apertures spanning ~3-4 revolutions with a median expansion of 1.54 per revolution), which limits discrimination between exponential and linear growth; the median RMSE ratio of 1.39 reflects that limited leverage as well as genuine departures.

Tenagodus is a siliquariid whose coiling loosens and uncoils in adulthood, so its non-logarithmic fit is expected; removing it does not change the gastropod percentage materially (it contributes 2 of 145 specimens).

The Fermat (parabolic) spiral, which modern work (Vogel 1979) uses for sunflower capitula, is the worst of the three models for every mollusc group here (median RMSE ratio 3-25), i.e. molluscs are not sunflower-like; the sunflower class itself could not be tested.
Dryad downloads are served behind a proof-of-work interstitial (Anubis); analysis.py completes it automatically and must download the 521 MB archive (only the 1.5 MB .tps inside is read).
